subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 9-month-old boy is referred for a rapidly enlarging abdomen and poor weight gain. Examination shows hepatosplenomegaly, mild hypotonia, and failure to thrive. Liver biopsy shows cirrhosis with accumulation of abnormally branched glycogen. Fasting glucose and lactate are normal at this stage.
question: Which of the following enzyme deficiencies is most likely responsible?
explanation_correct: Andersen disease (type IV) is caused by deficiency of branching enzyme, so glycogen with abnormally long, unbranched outer chains accumulates and incites cirrhosis. Infants present with hepatosplenomegaly and failure to thrive, and hypoglycemia tends to occur late in the disease.

explanation_incorrect.A: Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency (von Gierke disease) causes severe early fasting hypoglycemia with lactic acidosis and is not characterized by cirrhosis in infancy.
explanation_incorrect.B: Debranching enzyme deficiency (Cori disease) leads to limit dextrin accumulation and hepatomegaly, but cirrhosis and failure to thrive in early infancy are more typical of Andersen disease.
explanation_incorrect.C: Lysosomal acid alpha-1,4-glucosidase deficiency (Pompe disease) presents with cardiomyopathy and profound hypotonia rather than infantile cirrhosis.
explanation_incorrect.D: Muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency (McArdle disease) affects skeletal muscle only and does not involve the liver.

educationalObjective: Andersen disease (branching enzyme deficiency) presents in infancy with hepatosplenomegaly, failure to thrive, and cirrhosis from abnormally branched glycogen.
